intro: Mimì comes to her neighbour’s attic to have her candle lit and stays to tell him about her life. Claudia Muzio sings Puccini’s portrait of an embroiderer whose small room gets the first sun of spring.

sections.label: A · Mimì tells Rodolfo her name
sections.mNote: Short phrases grow into a song about flowers and poetry

sections.label: A′ · A room of her own
sections.mNote: The opening phrase returns, then the accompaniment skips along

sections.label: B · The first sun of spring
sections.mNote: A broad melody climbs towards D major

sections.label: Coda · The neighbour apologises
sections.mNote: Free, natural speech above a held chord

cues.title: Her name is Lucia
cues.text: “Mi chiamano Mimì, ma il mio nome è Lucia” — “They call me Mimì, but my name is Lucia.” Rodolfo has told her he is a poet. Sitting in his attic, she answers with her own work: embroidering lilies and roses on linen or silk.
cues.evidence: Illica and Giacosa, La bohème (1896), Act I: Mimì’s reply to Rodolfo. Ricordi vocal score, pp. 69–70, marks her opening con semplicità, still seated. Italian text: https://it.wikisource.org/wiki/La_boh%C3%A8me/Quadro_primo . Translation ours.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Lunch alone, prayers at home
cues.text: Mimì repeats her name, then talks about making her own lunch, praying and living alone in a little white room. Puccini lets her talk lightly: after the returning opening phrase, the score moves into Allegretto moderato, with a skipping accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Ricordi vocal score, pp. 71–72: renewed Mi chiamano Mimì marked Lentamente; Sola mi fo il pranzo da me stessa marked Allegretto moderato, con semplicità. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP885138-PMLP50378-puccini_mi_chiamano_mimi_from_la_boheme_ricordi.pdf.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A candle and a key
cues.text: Mimì’s candle goes out; she drops her key in Rodolfo’s room. He finds it and quietly pockets it, prolonging their search in the dark. By the time she begins this aria, he has held her cold hand and told her about his poems.
cues.evidence: Illica and Giacosa, La bohème (1896), Act I, candle-and-key scene preceding the two arias. https://it.wikisource.org/wiki/La_boh%C3%A8me/Quadro_primo

cues.title: The first sun is hers
cues.text: “Il primo sole è mio” — “The first sunshine is mine.” At the thought of spring, Mimì stands up. The music broadens into Andante molto sostenuto, and her voice climbs above an accompaniment that grows towards the D-major climax.
cues.evidence: Ricordi vocal score, p. 73: stage direction si alza, Andante molto sostenuto and con grande espansione at the climax. Illica and Giacosa’s Act I text; translation ours. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP885138-PMLP50378-puccini_mi_chiamano_mimi_from_la_boheme_ricordi.pdf.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Back to the small room
cues.text: The flowers Mimì embroiders have no scent. Her song quietens, and she apologises for disturbing her neighbour so late. Puccini marks the last explanation “senza rigore di tempo, con naturalezza” — “without strict time, naturally”. The soprano talks over a held chord.
cues.evidence: Ricordi vocal score, p. 74, final paragraph of Mimì’s aria: the embroidered flowers, her apology and Puccini’s tempo instruction. Translation ours. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP885138-PMLP50378-puccini_mi_chiamano_mimi_from_la_boheme_ricordi.pdf.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Mimì starts her introduction again
transitions.from: A · Mimì tells Rodolfo her name
transitions.to: A′ · A room of her own
transitions.how: The first song about flowers and poetry contracts into a brief exchange with Rodolfo. Mimì then repeats her introduction, marked Lentamente in 2/4. The rising phrase returns with chromatic notes and separated chords underneath; the soprano has room for pauses between her words.
transitions.evidence: Ricordi vocal score, p. 71: the renewed Mi chiamano Mimì, Lentamente in 2/4, with altered notes and separated accompaniment. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP885138-PMLP50378-puccini_mi_chiamano_mimi_from_la_boheme_ricordi.pdf.pdf

transitions.title: A pause before the spring sunshine
transitions.from: A′ · A room of her own
transitions.to: B · The first sun of spring
transitions.how: A held pause ends Mimì’s account of looking over the roofs. The metre opens into common time, marked Andante molto sostenuto. G-major harmony supports the new melody; the bass then moves through E and A towards the D-major climax. The soprano’s short sentences have become a long, rising song.
transitions.evidence: Ricordi vocal score, pp. 72–73: fermata, common-time Andante molto sostenuto, G-major opening and the E–A–D bass route to the climax. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP885138-PMLP50378-puccini_mi_chiamano_mimi_from_la_boheme_ricordi.pdf.pdf

transitions.title: A held chord lets Mimì speak
transitions.from: B · The first sun of spring
transitions.how: The earlier flower melody returns quietly. As Mimì explains that her embroidered flowers have no scent, the accompaniment settles into D major. Her final apology runs freely over the held chord, marked senza rigore di tempo, con naturalezza. A brief chord closes her introduction.
transitions.evidence: Ricordi vocal score, p. 74: the quiet melodic recall, sustained D-major chord and freely timed final explanation. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP885138-PMLP50378-puccini_mi_chiamano_mimi_from_la_boheme_ricordi.pdf.pdf

source.title: Puccini, La bohème, Act I, full orchestral score (Ricordi)
source.locator: Ricordi full score, PDF pp. 98–107: rehearsal figures 35–38, from Mimì’s introduction to her freely spoken final apology.

timeline.note: Quiet strings accompany Mimì’s introduction; flute, clarinet and harp add brief answers.
Divided strings accompany the song about flowers; woodwinds, harp and quiet percussion join its longer phrases.
Repeated string chords accompany the shorter phrases, with clarinet, bass clarinet and horns.
A solo viola plays beneath Mimì’s returning introduction; the winds are silent.
A flute skips above sparse string notes and harp chords as Mimì describes life alone.
Flute, clarinet and first violins sing the spring melody with Mimì; horns and low strings support them.
Flutes, horns and high strings double the broad vocal climax, with trumpets and trombones beneath.
The soprano climbs again, accompanied by upper winds, horn and divided strings.
Soft winds, harp and percussion quieten; muted strings accompany the return to conversation.
The strings hold a chord while Mimì makes her final apology freely, then add a short closing chord.

composer.epithet: He could make a whole theatre wait with a woman at a window, then break its heart with a tune it had heard before.
facts: Lucca; Milan Conservatory, 1880–83, with Bazzini and Ponchielli
Giulio Ricordi · Luigi Illica and Giuseppe Giacosa · Giuseppe Adami and Renato Simoni
Twelve operas, counting Il trittico as three; a Mass, songs and chamber music
composer.background:
Puccini began at the organ. His family had supplied Lucca with church musicians for generations, and when his father Michele died in 1864, the five-year-old Giacomo was expected to continue the trade. He studied in the town, played in its churches and completed a Mass in 1880. But in 1876 he had heard Verdi’s Aida in Pisa. The theatre won. A scholarship helped him into the Milan Conservatory, where Antonio Bazzini and Amilcare Ponchielli taught him composition. His graduation piece of 1883, Capriccio sinfonico, contains the bustling music that would eventually open La bohème.

His first opera nearly went nowhere. He submitted Le Villi to the Sonzogno competition on the last possible day, 31 December 1883; it failed even to receive a mention. The librettist Ferdinando Fontana arranged a private hearing at the journalist Marco Sala’s house, with Arrigo Boito among the guests. A subscription paid for a performance at Milan’s Teatro Dal Verme the following May. Giulio Ricordi bought the opera and commissioned another. Edgar, first performed at La Scala in 1889, was a failure that Puccini spent years trying to repair.
